subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: Tasting the Six Flavours of Ugadi Pachadi
periods.textbook_anchor: Mystery Masala — students think about and list dishes they would include in a school food festival (p. 73)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of the school food festival scene

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the Mystery Masala stall scenario from Textbook p. 73, pausing to let students picture a school food festival. Students share aloud one or two festival dishes from their own family or community.

The teacher introduces the six tastes — sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, astringent — writing each on the board alongside its Hindi term. Students recall any food that carries each taste and call out examples while the teacher lists them.

Students open Textbook p. 73 and work on the 'Think and Write' prompt: they list five dishes they would include in a school food festival. Pairs share their lists and notice which tastes their chosen dishes cover.

Whole-class discussion: the teacher asks which taste was hardest to find a dish for, and which dishes surprised students by having more than one taste. The class connects this variety of tastes to the idea that balanced food covers all six.
Closing thought: the teacher names Shad Rasa as the Ayurvedic term for the six-taste principle and invites students to notice all six tastes in one meal at home.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and categorise everyday food items according to a recognised system of sensory properties.
periods.section_context: Ugadi Pachadi, school food festival scenario, six tastes (sweet/meetha, sour/khatta, salty/namkeen, pungent/teekha, bitter/karva, astringent/kasaila), Shad Rasa.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone eaten something that had two or three different tastes at the same time — what was it like?' Draw out the idea that traditional dishes often blend tastes intentionally; invite students who know festive or regional dishes from their own families to share.

periods.activity_title: Mapping Five Foods to Each of the Six Tastes
periods.textbook_anchor: Mystery Masala — students write at least five ingredients or food items that match each of the six tastes (p. 74)

time_bands.activity: Quick recap: the teacher points to the six-taste words on the board (left from the exploration in the earlier food-festival discussion) and asks students to call out one food for each taste from memory, to activate what they already know.

Students open Textbook p. 74 and complete the 'Write' task independently — listing at least five ingredients or food items for each of the six tastes in the spaces provided. They draw on home experience, school meals, and regional foods they know.

Students form small groups (three to four) and compare their lists, then do the 'Discuss' task from Textbook p. 74: they identify food items in their combined lists that carry at least three different tastes simultaneously.
Groups share one multi-taste food item each. The teacher records these on the board and the class discusses how multi-taste foods might reflect the Shad Rasa idea of balance.
Students note one multi-taste food from today's discussion in their notebooks as a personal record.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the sensory properties of familiar items by sorting them into a systematic classification.
periods.section_context: Six tastes classification table, food items with multiple tastes, Shad Rasa balance principle, student-generated taste lists.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Can you think of a food that your family makes for a festival or celebration that has more than one taste — what makes it special?' This naturally surfaces regional and traditional foods without singling out any community.

periods.activity_title: Millets Through the Seasons — A 'Super Food' Inquiry
periods.textbook_anchor: A Stall of 'Super Food' — students find out more about a millet-based food prepared at their home (p. 75)
materials: Index cards or small paper slips (one per student)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of the millet stall

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the millet stall narrative from Textbook p. 75 aloud, pausing at the grandmother's seasonal food wisdom — jowar and bajra roti in winters, jau roti in summers. Students listen and identify which millets are named.

Brief class discussion: do students' families eat any grain that changes with the season? Students share examples; the teacher records the grain names on the board (millets and others) without correcting regional variety.

Students carry out the 'Find out' inquiry from Textbook p. 75 in-class as a structured recall task. On an index card they write: (a) one millet-based food made at home or known in their region, (b) when it is usually eaten, and (c) one reason a family member gave for eating it. Students who do not know a millet food may write about any traditional grain food from home.

Cards are shared in a gallery walk: students place cards on a desk and walk around reading two or three cards from classmates. The teacher highlights the variety of millets — jowar, bajra, jau — and their nutritional richness as described in the textbook.
Closing: the teacher asks why millets might be called 'super food' and invites students to name one nutrient idea they heard today.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple inquiry by gathering and reporting information about a familiar food practice from their home or community.
periods.section_context: Millets — jowar, bajra, jau; seasonal food wisdom (winter/summer consumption); millet stall narrative; nutritional richness of millets.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What did your grandmother or an elder at home tell you about why they ate a particular food in a particular season?' This draws out traditional seasonal food knowledge naturally; celebrate all regional answers as equally valid.

periods.activity_title: Sorting Foods into Three Groups that Keep Us Healthy
periods.textbook_anchor: How Does Food Help Us? — students discuss why we need to eat different kinds of food items (p. 75)
materials: Three-column sorting chart drawn on board
periods.visual_aids: Textbook diagram of the three food groups

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses the discussion question from Textbook p. 75: 'Why do we need to eat different kinds of food items?' Students think quietly for a moment, then share ideas. The teacher captures key words — energy, growth, protection — on the board.

The teacher introduces the three food groups using the textbook content: energy-giving (rice, wheat, potato, millets, ghee), body-building (pulses, milk, eggs, meat, fish), and protective (fruits and vegetables like carrot, orange, spinach, amla). Students open Textbook p. 75 and follow along, then copy the three-column chart into their notebooks with the listed examples.
Students extend the chart by adding two more foods they eat regularly to each column, using their own judgement. Pairs compare additions and justify their choices to each other.

The teacher facilitates a short discussion using the second prompt from Textbook p. 77: 'What will happen if we eat food from a single group every day?' Students reason through consequences for energy, growth, and health.
Students write one sentence in their notebooks: 'Eating from all three groups is important because …' completing it in their own words.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify food items into functional categories based on their role in the body.
periods.section_context: Three food groups — energy-giving (rice, wheat, potato, millets, ghee), body-building (pulses, milk, eggs, meat, fish), protective (carrot, orange, spinach, amla); consequences of eating from a single group.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If someone ate only rice and bread for a week, what might happen to their body — and what would be missing?' Prompt students to use the group names (energy-giving, body-building, protective) in their reasoning rather than just naming foods.

periods.activity_title: Our Regional Thali — A Window into Balanced Eating
periods.textbook_anchor: How Does Food Help Us? — students find out a food thali from their region and list its food items (p. 80)
materials: Board space for class thali map
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image of India's regional food thalis

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 80 and draws students' attention to the regional thali images. Students observe quietly and name any thali item they recognise from their own family meals.

Students carry out the 'Find out' task from Textbook p. 80 in-class: they recall or describe a food thali from their own region and list its items in their notebook. For each item they label it with its food group — energy-giving, body-building, or protective — using what they learned about the three groups.

Small groups (three to four) share their regional thali lists. Together they check: does the thali include items from all three food groups? They discuss why a thali might naturally contain all three.

Whole-class connection: the teacher asks how regional food traditions became naturally balanced without people necessarily knowing the three-group system. Students connect this to the earlier discussion about Shad Rasa and seasonal wisdom.
Students write one observation in their notebooks: which food group was most represented in their regional thali, and which was least.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect a cultural food practice to a functional framework by identifying which food groups a traditional meal covers.
periods.section_context: Regional food thalis from India, three food groups classification applied to thali items, connection between cultural food diversity and nutritional balance.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does the thali your family eats change between different occasions — a festival meal vs an everyday meal?' This surfaces both cultural diversity and the idea that balance looks different in different traditions; accept all regional examples as valid.

periods.activity_title: Recognising and Reasoning Against Junk Food
periods.textbook_anchor: Say 'No' to Junk Food — students write why we should avoid eating junk food (p. 78)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image of junk food items

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 78 and reads the junk food section aloud. Students look at the examples illustrated — soft drinks, chips, bread pakoda, burgers, pizza — and name other packaged or processed foods they see in shops or eat occasionally.

Students complete the first 'Write' task from Textbook p. 78: they name a few more junk food items beyond those listed. The teacher collects examples on the board, noting the shared features — high oil, salt, or sugar content.

Students complete the second 'Write' task from Textbook p. 78: they write why we should avoid eating junk food, drawing on what they know about the three food groups and what the body needs. Pairs read each other's reasons and add any point they missed.

Students complete the third 'Write' task from Textbook p. 78: they list junk food items they personally will aim to avoid. The teacher frames this as a personal commitment, not a rule imposed from outside, and asks students to think about one fresh or home-cooked alternative for each item they list.
Whole-class reflection: the teacher asks, 'Is it possible to enjoy occasional treats and still eat a healthy diet?' Students share briefly; the tone closes on balanced choice rather than prohibition.

periods.implied_lo: Students can evaluate food choices by applying criteria about nutritional harm and justify a personal commitment to healthier alternatives.
periods.section_context: Junk food definition (high oil, salt, sugar), examples (soft drinks, chips, bread pakoda, burgers, pizza, packaged food), contrast with fresh home-cooked food, personal avoidance list.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What does someone in your family cook at home that you enjoy just as much as packaged snacks — and what makes it different?' This steers the discussion toward positive food choices without shaming any student's eating habits.

periods.activity_title: Designing a Balanced Plate and Starting a Food Diary
periods.textbook_anchor: A Balanced Food Plate — students create a food diary of their daily routine for a week, noting healthy and unhealthy items and identifying missing food groups (p. 79)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook diagram of the balanced food plate portions

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 79 and discusses the balanced plate: protective foods (fruits and vegetables) form the largest portion, followed by body-building foods, then energy-giving foods. Students sketch a rough plate diagram in their notebooks with the three portions labelled.

Students open Textbook p. 79 and begin Activity 1 in class: they set up a food diary grid in their notebook for today's meals — breakfast, lunch, and dinner — and write what they ate or plan to eat. They encircle items that are healthy and mark items that are not healthy with an X.

Students review their diary entry and identify which food groups are present and which are missing. They write one sentence noting what their plate was missing and one suggestion for an ingredient that would fill that gap.

Small-group discussion: students share one missing food group and the suggested addition. The group discusses whether the addition is realistic for their family — affordable, locally available, familiar in taste.

The teacher explains that students are encouraged to continue the diary for the rest of the week at home with a parent or family member, as the textbook suggests — but today's work stands complete on its own.

periods.implied_lo: Students can evaluate the nutritional completeness of a real meal by applying a structured food-group framework and identifying gaps.
periods.section_context: Balanced food plate (protective foods largest portion, then body-building, then energy-giving), food diary with breakfast/lunch/dinner, healthy/unhealthy marking, missing food group identification.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If your plate had no protective foods today, what is one colourful vegetable or fruit your family usually has at home that you could add?' Grounding the gap-filling in what is actually available at home keeps the task realistic and non-judgmental.

periods.activity_title: Water as a Hidden Essential — How Much Is Enough?
periods.textbook_anchor: Water for Health — students discuss how water supports digestion, skin health, and waste removal, and how water-rich fruits contribute to hydration

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Is water a food? Where would you put it on the balanced plate we drew?' Students debate briefly. The teacher then reads the Water for Health section from the textbook, which presents water as an essential companion to food.

Class discussion on water's roles: the teacher guides students through how water aids digestion, keeps skin healthy, and removes waste through urine, sweat, and faeces. Students note these three roles in their notebooks with a simple diagram (arrow from 'water' to each role).

The teacher introduces the idea of water-rich foods — watermelon, cucumber — as an additional source of hydration. Students recall any water-rich foods they know from their region and add them to their notes. The class discusses why eating these foods helps on hot days or after exercise.

Students reflect individually: how much water did they drink today, and at which points in the day? They write two habits they could change to drink more water — for example, keeping a bottle at the desk or eating a water-rich food at lunch.
Closing: the teacher summarises that water is as important as food for health, and that it comes both from drinking and from the food we eat.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe the specific roles of a substance in the body and connect everyday habits to those biological functions.
periods.section_context: Water's roles (digestion, skin health, waste removal through urine/sweat/faeces), water-rich fruits (watermelon, cucumber), daily water intake as a health habit.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What do people in very hot parts of India or during summer festivals do to stay cool and hydrated — do you know of any drink or food from your region that helps?' This naturally surfaces regional food and seasonal health wisdom.

periods.activity_title: How Is It Cooked? Matching Foods to Their Cooking Methods
periods.textbook_anchor: Different Methods of Cooking — students identify different methods used to cook food items from a given list (p. 81)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook list of food items and cooking methods on p. 81

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'How many different ways does your family cook food?' Students call out methods; the teacher lists them on the board. The class then opens Textbook p. 81 to see the six named methods: boiling, steaming, roasting, grilling, frying, and baking.

Students complete the 'Write' task from Textbook p. 81: they identify the cooking method for each food item in the textbook list, using the example given. They may consult family members' knowledge they carry with them and add more items to the list with their cooking method.
Pairs compare their completed lists. Where they disagree on a method for the same food, they discuss why — some foods can be cooked more than one way — and note both methods.

The teacher introduces the two facts from the textbook: the meaning of 'Chef' in French, and the use of solar cookers as an environment-friendly cooking method. Students discuss briefly what makes solar cooking sustainable.
Students note one food from their own home that can be eaten without any cooking (e.g. fruit chaat, salad) and write why eating some raw foods is good for health.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the preparation method associated with familiar foods and identify patterns across cooking techniques.
periods.section_context: Cooking methods (boiling, steaming, roasting, grilling, frying, baking), food items matched to methods, foods eaten without cooking (fruit chaat, vegetable salad), solar cookers, meaning of 'Chef'.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does your family use a cooking method not on this list — perhaps one used for a special dish or festival food?' This surfaces regional cooking traditions such as smoking, pit roasting, or stone grinding; validate all answers as genuine knowledge.

periods.activity_title: Cooking Is for Everyone — Discussion and Reflection
periods.textbook_anchor: Different Methods of Cooking — students discuss whether all family members should know how to cook and why (p. 82)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 82 and poses the first discussion question: 'Do you help in cooking at home?' Students share briefly — what they do, who taught them, and how it felt. The teacher notes the variety of responses without assigning value to whether students help or not.

Small groups (four to five) discuss the second question from Textbook p. 82: 'Do you think all family members should know how to cook? Why?' Groups are asked to reach a shared position and prepare two reasons to support it.

Groups share their positions. The teacher facilitates a whole-class conversation about division of labour at home, gender, and the practical value of cooking as a life skill for everyone. The teacher draws out that cooking knowledge is both a cultural tradition and a practical necessity.
Individual reflection: students write two to three sentences in their notebook expressing their own view on whether all family members should cook, and one thing they would like to learn to cook.
Closing: the teacher affirms that cooking is a valued skill that connects people to their food, their culture, and their health.

periods.implied_lo: Students can articulate a reasoned personal view on a social practice and connect it to values of shared responsibility and care.
periods.section_context: Helping in cooking at home, whether all family members should cook, division of labour and cooking as a life skill, personal cooking aspirations.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there a dish in your family that only one person knows how to make — and what would happen if that person was not there?' This opens a natural conversation about shared food knowledge and the value of passing cooking skills across all family members.

periods.activity_title: Food Collage — Classifying the Foods We Know
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — students cut out pictures of food items and create a collage with three sections for the three food groups (p. 83)
materials: Old magazines, newspapers, or food packaging with pictures
A sheet of paper or notebook page

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 83 and explains the food collage task: students will create a three-section collage labelled energy-giving, body-building, and protective, placing cut-out food pictures in the correct section. Students divide their paper into three sections and label them.

Students cut out or draw food pictures and arrange them into the three sections of their collage, using Textbook p. 83 as a reference. They aim for at least three food items per section. Where students draw rather than cut, they label each item clearly.

Students do a brief gallery walk: they place their collage on their desk and walk around to see two classmates' collages. They use a simple prompt — 'I agree with this placement' or 'I would move this because …' — to engage with each other's classification choices.

Students complete the food word-search from Textbook p. 84, circling food-related vocabulary. The teacher closes by asking: 'Looking at your collage and today's chapter, what is one food habit you want to carry forward?' Students share one word or phrase.

periods.implied_lo: Students can organise and present their understanding of a classification system through a self-made visual product.
periods.section_context: Food collage with three sections (energy-giving, body-building, protective), cut-out or drawn food pictures, food word-search grid.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there any food in your collage that could go into more than one group — and how would you decide where to place it?' This extends thinking beyond simple sorting toward understanding that some foods serve multiple functions.

assessment_items.question_text: Ugadi Pachadi is described as having six different tastes. Which of the following is NOT one of the six tastes named in this tradition?
assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is C. 'Spicy (masaledar)' is not one of the six Shad Rasa tastes; the six are sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent. All distractors are drawn directly from the six-taste list in the section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and categorise everyday food items according to a recognised system of sensory properties.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'astringent (kasaila)' suggests the student was unsure whether astringent is a recognised taste category and guessed it was not included — it is one of the six.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'pungent (teekha)' suggests confusion between pungent and spicy, treating them as the same thing and therefore thinking pungent does not belong — it does.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'bitter (karva)' suggests the student associated bitter with an unpleasant or unhealthy taste and assumed it would not be included in a positive food tradition — it is one of the six.

assessment_items.question_text: A student lists the six tastes and tries to find a food item that matches each taste. She easily finds foods for sweet, sour, and salty — but struggles with bitter and astringent. Name one food item for bitter taste and one for astringent taste, and explain what the Shad Rasa principle says about having all six tastes in a balanced meal.
expected_elements: A plausible food example for bitter taste (e.g. karela/bitter gourd, methi/fenugreek, neem leaves).
A plausible food example for astringent taste (e.g. amla/gooseberry, raw banana, pomegranate skin, turmeric).
A statement that Shad Rasa refers to the six-taste principle from Ayurveda.
A statement that balanced food containing all six tastes is considered good for health.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any regionally familiar food that carries bitter or astringent taste — there is no single correct example. A complete response names a plausible food for each taste and links the six-taste system to the Ayurvedic idea of health. Regional-variation note: students may name different regional foods for bitter and astringent — e.g. raw jackfruit, unripe guava, or local greens — all are acceptable if the taste is correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the sensory properties of familiar items by sorting them into a systematic classification.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

expected_elements: A plausible food example for bitter taste (e.g. karela/bitter gourd, methi/fenugreek, neem leaves).
A plausible food example for astringent taste (e.g. amla/gooseberry, raw banana, pomegranate skin, turmeric).
A statement that Shad Rasa refers to the six-taste principle from Ayurveda.
A statement that balanced food containing all six tastes is considered good for health.

assessment_items.question_text: A grandmother eats jowar and bajra roti in winters and jau roti in summers. What does this seasonal food practice tell us about millets, and why might this traditional knowledge be useful for us today?
expected_elements: Recognition that millets such as jowar, bajra, and jau are nutrient-rich foods.
A statement that the grandmother's choice shows seasonal food wisdom — different millets suit different seasons.
A statement connecting this traditional practice to the idea that millets are healthy, sustainable food choices.
A reason why this knowledge is useful today — e.g. millets are nutritious, locally available, or part of a balanced diet.
assessment_items.annotation: A complete response identifies seasonal variation in millet use, names at least one millet, and makes a connection to health or sustainability. Regional-variation note: students may refer to millets or traditional grains by local names — accept all regionally accurate equivalents.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple inquiry by gathering and reporting information about a familiar food practice from their home or community.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

A statement that the grandmother's choice shows seasonal food wisdom — different millets suit different seasons.
A statement connecting this traditional practice to the idea that millets are healthy, sustainable food choices.
A reason why this knowledge is useful today — e.g. millets are nutritious, locally available, or part of a balanced diet.

assessment_items.question_text: Riya wants to grow strong muscles and repair her body after a long day of play. Which food group should she eat MORE of to support body-building?

options.label: A
options.text: Body-building foods like pulses, milk, and eggs

options.label: B
options.text: Energy-giving foods like rice and potato

options.label: C
options.text: Junk foods like chips and soft drinks

options.label: D
options.text: Protective foods like carrot and spinach

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. Body-building foods (pulses, milk, eggs, meat, fish) support muscle growth and repair. Distractors A and C represent the other two food groups from the same chapter section; D is a chapter-level concept (junk food) that reinforces understanding of what not to eat.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify food items into functional categories based on their role in the body.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing energy-giving foods suggests the student confused the function of energy provision with body repair and growth — a common mix-up between the two most frequently discussed food groups.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing protective foods suggests the student associated 'protection' with physical strength, not understanding that protective foods guard against disease rather than build muscle.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing junk foods suggests the student has not connected the chapter's food-group framework to the question, or has not retained that junk food harms rather than helps the body.

assessment_items.question_text: Meena describes her family's regional thali: it has chapati, dal, sabzi, and a small piece of fish. Identify which food group each item belongs to and explain whether this thali is balanced or not.
expected_elements: Chapati (or wheat-based bread) correctly identified as an energy-giving food.
Dal (lentils/pulses) correctly identified as a body-building food.
Sabzi (vegetable dish) correctly identified as a protective food.
Fish correctly identified as a body-building food.
A judgement that the thali is reasonably balanced, with items from all three groups.
Optional: a note that a fruit or extra vegetable could strengthen the protective food presence.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any plausible regional thali described in the student's own context. Regional-variation note: thali components vary widely across India; students who describe a thali from their own region with different items should be assessed on whether they correctly apply the three food groups, not on whether the items match this example.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect a cultural food practice to a functional framework by identifying which food groups a traditional meal covers.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

Dal (lentils/pulses) correctly identified as a body-building food.
Sabzi (vegetable dish) correctly identified as a protective food.
Fish correctly identified as a body-building food.
A judgement that the thali is reasonably balanced, with items from all three groups.
Optional: a note that a fruit or extra vegetable could strengthen the protective food presence.

assessment_items.question_text: Your friend says, 'Chips and soft drinks taste great and give me energy, so they must be good for my health.' Do you agree or disagree? Give reasons using what you know about junk food and healthy eating.
look_for: A clear position — the student disagrees with the friend's claim.
A definition or description of junk food as food high in oil, salt, or sugar that is harmful when eaten regularly.
A distinction between providing calories/energy and being nutritionally healthy.
At least one specific harm of regular junk food consumption mentioned.
A suggestion of a healthier alternative that could be eaten in place of chips or soft drinks.
Use of food-group language (energy-giving, body-building, or protective) to strengthen the argument.
assessment_items.annotation: A strong response disagrees clearly, defines junk food, distinguishes energy from nutrition, names at least one harm, and suggests an alternative. A weak response either agrees with the friend or disagrees without reasoning. Full marks require use of food-group or nutritional vocabulary from the chapter.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate food choices by applying criteria about nutritional harm and justify a personal commitment to healthier alternatives.

assessment_items.task: Look at what you ate for breakfast and lunch today. Draw your balanced plate: divide a circle into three sections — one large section for protective foods, one medium section for body-building foods, and one smaller section for energy-giving foods. In each section, write or draw the foods from today's meals that belong there. If a section is empty, write one food you could add to fill it.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My balanced plate:
- Largest section (Protective foods — fruits and vegetables): ___
- Middle section (Body-building foods — pulses, milk, eggs, meat, fish): ___
- Smallest section (Energy-giving foods — rice, wheat, potato, ghee): ___
Missing group(s): ___
One food I could add: ___
format_of_output: A labelled circle diagram divided into three sections
Written food items placed in the correct section
One suggested addition for any empty section
assessment_items.annotation: Assess whether the student correctly applies the three-section plate model to real meal data, accurately places foods in the right sections, and identifies a genuine gap. A strong response shows all three sections labelled, foods placed correctly, and a realistic, regionally appropriate suggestion for any missing group. Regional-variation note: meal contents vary widely; assess the classification logic, not the specific foods named.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate the nutritional completeness of a real meal by applying a structured food-group framework and identifying gaps.

competency.competency_text: Describes the basic safety needs and protection (health and hygiene, food, water, shelter, precautions, awareness of emergency situations, abuse, and unsafe situations) of humans, birds, and animals

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can apply the balanced-plate framework to a real, personal meal and identify nutritional gaps — demonstrating that food-group knowledge transfers to everyday eating decisions.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts the student to move section by section through their own plate; a student who leaves all three scaffold lines blank for 'missing group' may not have understood the concept of a gap, while one who fills sections with foods from the wrong group has a classification error to address.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: three sections correctly labelled, at least one food per section that is genuinely present in the student's meal, a plausible and realistic food added for any empty section. Weak: sections unlabelled or confused, foods placed in the wrong group without adjustment, no attempt to identify a missing group.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who do not eat eggs, meat, or fish can identify body-building foods through pulses, legumes, or dairy. Students who ate no vegetables may simply note the protective section is empty and suggest a fruit or vegetable from their region. Drawing the plate instead of writing labels is equally valid.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Labelled circle diagram with written or drawn food items and a written addition
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The plate diagram mirrors the textbook's balanced-plate visual, making the classification concrete and directly connected to the chapter content.

assessment_items.question_text: Water helps the body remove waste in three main ways. Which of the following is NOT one of those ways?
assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is C. The textbook names urine, sweat, and faeces as the three ways water removes waste. Tears are not listed. All distractors are drawn from the section's content: A, B, and D are all correct ways named in the chapter; C is a plausible body fluid that students may assume is included.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe the specific roles of a substance in the body and connect everyday habits to those biological functions.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing urine suggests the student may have memorised only one of the three waste-removal routes and incorrectly treated a correct answer as the 'not included' option — a reading comprehension gap.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing sweat suggests confusion about the body's cooling and waste-removal mechanisms; the student may not have noticed that sweat is explicitly listed in the section.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing faeces suggests the student associated waste removal with digestion only and assumed faeces is unrelated to water — the section explicitly links all three to water's role in the body.

assessment_items.question_text:
Look at the list of food items below. Write the cooking method most commonly used for each item. You may name more than one method if it applies.

| Food item | Cooking method |
|---|---|
| Rice | |
| Idli | |
| Roti | |
| Fish | |
| Cake | |
expected_elements: Rice: boiling (accept steaming as a valid alternative).
Idli: steaming.
Roti: roasting or grilling on a tawa (accept both).
Fish: frying or grilling (accept both; accept regional methods such as steaming).
Cake: baking.
At least four out of five correct to demonstrate the pattern across methods.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept regionally common cooking methods for each item — for example, fish may be steamed in some regions and fried in others. Regional-variation note: the method for fish, roti, and rice can differ meaningfully by region; assess whether the method named is genuinely used for that food, not whether it matches the textbook example exactly.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the preparation method associated with familiar foods and identify patterns across cooking techniques.

assessment_items.question_text: In many homes, only one or two people do all the cooking. Do you think all members of a family — including children — should learn how to cook? Give at least two reasons for your view and explain how knowing how to cook can be useful in everyday life.
look_for: A clear personal position — yes or no, with an acknowledgement that the question involves real choices.
At least two distinct reasons supporting the position (e.g. cooking as a life skill, shared responsibility at home, understanding what goes into food, cultural connection, independence).
At least one example of a specific everyday situation where cooking knowledge is useful.
Some acknowledgement of the idea that cooking is not limited to one gender or one person in a family.
Language that is respectful of different family arrangements.
assessment_items.annotation: A strong response takes a clear position, offers at least two well-developed reasons, and provides a concrete everyday example. A weak response gives a single vague reason or avoids taking a position. There is no single correct view; assess the quality of reasoning, not the conclusion.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can articulate a reasoned personal view on a social practice and connect it to values of shared responsibility and care.

assessment_items.task: Create a food collage in your notebook. Draw or write the names of at least nine food items — three in each of the three sections below. For each item, write the food group it belongs to (energy-giving, body-building, or protective) and one reason why it belongs there.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Section 1 — Energy-giving foods:
1. ___ — belongs here because ___
2. ___ — belongs here because ___
3. ___ — belongs here because ___

Section 2 — Body-building foods:
1. ___ — belongs here because ___
2. ___ — belongs here because ___
3. ___ — belongs here because ___

Section 3 — Protective foods:
1. ___ — belongs here because ___
2. ___ — belongs here because ___
3. ___ — belongs here because ___
format_of_output: A three-section layout in the notebook (drawn or written)
At least nine food items placed across three sections
A brief reason for each item's placement
assessment_items.annotation: Assess whether the student correctly assigns foods to groups and provides a coherent reason for each placement. Strong responses will show variety across groups and use functional language ('gives energy', 'helps build muscles', 'protects from illness'). Regional-variation note: food items will vary by region; assess the classification rationale, not the specific foods chosen.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can organise and present their understanding of a classification system through a self-made visual product.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can recall, classify, and justify the placement of foods into the three food groups, demonstrating that the classification system is understood well enough to be applied independently to self-chosen examples.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: A student who fills all three sections with foods from only one group (e.g. all grains) has not internalised the three-group distinction. A student who places a protective food in the energy-giving section may have confused the groups; check whether the reason given reveals the confusion.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: nine foods correctly distributed, reasons use functional language about what each food does in the body, variety of food types within each section. Weak: fewer than nine items, foods misclassified with no supporting reason, or reasons are generic ('it is healthy') without reference to the group's function.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may draw food items rather than writing names; labelling in any language they are comfortable with is acceptable. Students who are unfamiliar with certain foods may substitute regional equivalents — a regional grain as energy-giving, local legumes as body-building, seasonal local vegetables as protective.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Three-section notebook layout with written food names or drawings and brief written reasons
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The three-section collage format directly mirrors the Let us reflect activity in the textbook, making the task a direct application of the chapter's closing reflective task.
